title: Childhood Psychological Maltreatment as a Predictor of Diminished Life Satisfaction in Early Adulthood
abstract: ABSTRACT Child maltreatment (CM) is consistently associated with chronic disease and disability, mental health‐related issues, and poorer quality of life. However, most research examining long‐term outcomes has focused on physical and sexual abuse, overlooking the distinct effect of childhood psychological maltreatment (CPM), particularly on subjective well‐being, a construct essential for recognizing the global impact of CM. Our cross‐sectional study examined the association between CM type and satisfaction with life among a sample of 503 young adults recruited from a university sample using correlational and hierarchical regression analysis. CPM was associated with the largest differences in life satisfaction across severity levels ( r = −0.49). Findings from regression analyses indicated that CPM was associated with significantly lower satisfaction with life and was the only maltreatment variable that remained a statistically significant predictor when all variables were considered. Implications for counseling research and practice are discussed.
